body.text: Indonesia has faced a whirlwind of economic challenges in 2026. The rupiah has steadily declined, making imports more expensive and fueling inflationary pressure. The stock market has seen big capital outflows and is looking at a major downgrade from global index provider MSCI. Borrowing costs are up, and recent opinion surveys show growing public concern about cost of living increases and the government’s ability to handle the issue.

What’s interesting about the current state of the Indonesian economy is that this feeling of economic malaise is somewhat at odds with key economic indicators and data. GDP growth, for instance, remains steady at around 5 percent. Monthly PMI data, which gauges whether manufacturing activity is expanding or contracting, reached a 31-month high in November. Auto sales are up 10 percent compared to the same period last year.

We are seeing a similar disconnect in the stock market, which has been absolutely pummeled this year. The Indonesian stock market has been one of the worst-performing exchanges in the world in 2026, with hundreds of billions of dollars in value wiped out thanks to sustained sell-offs. And yet, the largest listed companies are recording huge profits and generating billions of dollars in dividends for shareholders.

Bank Rakyat Indonesia and Bank Mandiri are two of the most valuable publicly listed companies on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX). In the first three quarters of 2026, Mandiri recorded net profit of IDR 47 trillion. Bank Rakyat Indonesia, which has a mandate to make loans to small businesses and rural borrowers, recorded IDR 48 trillion in net income.

The two banks together paid approximately $5.3 billion in dividends to their shareholders, the largest of which is state-owned investment fund Danantara, over the first nine months of the year. This is in line with recent performance, where these banks have been consistent and reliable dividend-generating machines. Non-performing rates are low, and customer deposits are growing, which suggests people are not burning through their savings or defaulting en masse.

And yet, shares in Bank Mandiri and Bank Rakyat Indonesia are being dragged down by the market, trading at price to earnings ratios of around 7 or lower. That is very low for consistently profitable banks with sound balance sheets. Somewhere there is a disconnect between the vibes and the data. How can the economy be growing and big listed companies generating solid returns, while stock prices crash, the currency drops, and people worry about cost of living and finding work?

It comes down largely to credibility and governance, two things that are hard to define and practically impossible to measure but which everyone has some intrinsic sense of. The economy is growing, but the government continually introduces uncertainty through new policies and announcements that challenge markets and investors, most recently in statements regarding greater state control over commodities and natural resources.

Fiscal policy has also been a flashpoint for negative sentiment with plenty of people questioning whether resources are being distributed equitably, and taking a hard look at who is really bearing the costs and enjoying the benefits of economic growth. It seems that 2026 will be better than 2025, at least in terms of overall fiscal health, but the way the government is raising and spending money is creating undercurrents of doubt despite reasonable headline numbers.

This dynamic is mirrored in the stock market. Bank Mandiri and Bank Rakyat Indonesia have healthy financials and return significant value to shareholders, but they were allowed to operate on the exchange next to companies that were valued way above what the underlying financials could justify.

This gets right to the heart of credibility and governance concerns, because it raises doubts about the ability of the exchange to price any Indonesian company correctly. The ensuing uncertainty has led to an ongoing correction that is dragging all valuations down, even for seemingly healthy companies.

It is hard to define credibility and governance with precision but businesses, consumers and investors know it when they see it. And what they are seeing now is an economy that displays surface-level signs of growth, but they are unsure about where things are headed. Public polling, sentiment surveys, prices and exchange rates are all mechanisms by which consumers, investors and businesses communicate their expectations. And right now they are sending a pretty clear message that they want more certainty and credibility.
